procedure: propose presentation content from a source document, review and fact-check it, then build the deck
why: One procedure: propose the slide content from a named source, have it fact-checked against that source and cut to a slide limit, confirm the format, build the deck. The review prompt ("Two things. Check every …") is a checkpoint on the proposal it refers to — "the slides" — not a new job; proposing, checking and building are one request driven through conversation. Ground truth stated by the person who ran it before any pipeline output was scored: one session, one process. Source: LEARNINGS.md, Part 1; agent claude-sonnet-5. Recorded without clearing concept_buddy between runs, so later runs saw earlier decks and Claude's project memory — realistic, and a confound for similarity.
history: Live capture: run 1 banked one candidate only because the judge timed out at the review gap; run 2 split at "Two things"; run 3 stayed whole. Replayed warm at temperature 0 the judge answers "new job" at the review prompt in all three — the whole runs were timeouts, not verdicts. It sees the request ("Don't build anything yet") and the review prompt, never the slides the prompt refers to.

input.text: I need to give a 10-minute talk to the team about what we learned working with an AI coding assistant on Concept Buddy. The material is in LEARNINGS.md, Part 1. Propose the content for the slides — titles and key points per slide. Don't build anything yet.

steps.reply:
Read Part 1. Propose 9 slides.

**1. Title** — "Working with an AI Coding Assistant: What We Learned Building Concept Buddy"

**2. Frame** — One line: two lessons mixed in project (assistant-use vs agent-design), today = assistant-use half. Core theme: "give AI less room to guess."

**3. Give it docs, not memory** — Claude coded structural change w/o framework docs wired in → worked from memory, built against grain → big rewrite. Rule: before structural work, ask "can it verify, or is it guessing?" Read enough yourself to spot wrong direction. Quote: "Blind acceptance is the expensive part. Not the AI."

**4. Scope, purpose, stopping point** — "write tests," no scope given → wildly oversized suite, later thrown out. Brief like a new dev: what/why/done/don't-touch. Quote: negative half of brief is cheap half.

**5. Small changes aren't small** — Moved one rule, same wording, different position → pass rate 4/5 → 2/5. Reason: instructions read in sequence, rule now lands after tools not before. Lesson: commit small, so you can isolate which line.

**6. One agent, many skills** — Skills-on-demand over multi-agent team: main instruction 11,785→5,422 chars, loading skill = unlocking its tools. Cost: "loaded" state resets per-turn → skill silently vanished turn 2 → looked like frontend bug for days, was 2 curl calls. Fix: once loaded in convo, stays armed.

**7. Question the plan, verify the result** — Rhythm: Explore→Plan→Question→Implement→Verify. Verify = most-skipped (ties to slide 3 cost). Question = most-rushed — reject alternatives in writing so decision doesn't reopen later. Quote: vague "why not X" answer = vague plan.

**8. Recap — one-slide version** (5 bullets, titles only, for people who read one slide): docs not memory / scope+purpose+stop / small changes aren't small / one agent many skills / question+verify.

**9. Close** — Common thread across all 5: less room to guess, more room to check.

Order = as-written in LEARNINGS.md; matches 10-min pace (~1 slide/min + buffer). Want me to trim, merge slide 2 into title, or add a slide w/ Part 2/3 teaser for follow-up talk?
